note:
Reviewed CDB90 match 160, pinned revision e0b35ec4d798cec3bb4e6970c0f6bb7aa69e2f4c. CDB90 (CAA Database of Battles, Version 1990), tidy data maintained by Jeffrey B. Arnold. Original US Army Concepts Analysis Agency data; revised data licensed ODC-BY. Original force designations and strength interpretations are retained with each quantity. Each side is one aggregate force, including any coalition; its total is not allocated among members. Personnel casualties are not deaths. Source estimates and adjudged error margins are not statistical confidence intervals. Equipment and tactical movements are not established by this dataset. Match review: Approve the whole 17–18 April 1847 battle after restoring the opening day. The Library of Congress catalogues the contemporary McClellan/Turnbull map explicitly for both days; U.S. Army CMH identifies Scott against Santa Anna’s entrenched army (about 12000), while AMEDD dates the victory to 18 April. CDB90 initial estimates remain 8500 U.S./12000 Mexican personnel. Its 431/4000 casualty figures are not deaths. CMH instead reports 64 U.S. killed+353 wounded and about 1000–1200 Mexican casualties separately from about 3000 prisoners; these differently tabulated estimates are disclosed, not substituted, summed into deaths, or assumed exactly equal to CDB90. Both source strength rows have no reinforcements. Identity review (attacker; original CDB90 name US ARMY): CMH identifies Scott’s U.S. army advancing through Cerro Gordo. The CDB90 quantity is the initial battle force, not all U.S. troops in Mexico. Historical published participant Q30 is replaced by this event-local aggregate; its exact original item and P710 statement citations are preserved here as provenance. It is not an additional separately scaled component. Identity review (defender; original CDB90 name MEX ARMY): CMH identifies Santa Anna’s entrenched army at this pass, estimated there at about 12000. This is an event-local force, not the country’s entire armed forces.

Cerro Gordo receives separately reviewed U.S. and Mexican infantry components. The Mexican blue/red tailcoat and light trousers are a war-period clothing analogy; regimental facings, supply, militia dress and weapons varied. Bustamante preserves partisan contemporary reports: their numerical claims, judgments and exact regimental enumeration are not adopted. Neither model describes a universal uniform or the whole composition of either army. The local participant ID, aggregate name, membership and CDB quantities remain unchanged. No infantry proportion or additional strength, casualty or death count is inferred.
